sections.title: Policy and access to the centre
sections.text: Apeldoorn, in Gelderland, charges for parking in zones that get cheaper with distance from the centre. The council adopted the parking tax ordinance for 2026 on 18 December 2025. Street parking costs 3.73 euros an hour in the high inner-city zone, with a two-hour maximum, 3.21 euros in the middle zone and 0.53 euro in the neighbourhoods [0]. Lots cost 3.21 euros an hour at Rosariumstraat with a daily maximum of 17.91 euros, 2.67 euros at Sprengenweg and P.W.A.-Laan, and 11.11 euros per 24 hours for campers [1]. A resident permit in the inner city costs 12.84 euros a month, and the enforcement charge is 82.00 euros [3]. The five municipal garages have been designated areas where permit holders may park since 2021, because there are too few street spaces for all residents, businesses and visitors [4]. The Beleidsregels Parkeren 2024 require developers to cover their own parking demand and aim to reduce the role of the car in the Binnenstad, Spoorzone and Kanaalzone; in the inner city a developer can transfer demand within about 400 metres to an existing municipal facility for 12,000 euros per space, and a mobility correction of up to 20 percent is possible [5][6]. The 2026 to 2029 budget proposes raising the parking tax on street and surface parking from 1 January 2027 through tariff differentiation, worth 160,000 euros a year, and we did not find the vote result [16].

sections.title: Parking developments
sections.text: The development to watch is the Vlijtseweg garage in the Kanaalzone. A final tender specification of 11 February 2026 calls for 584 parking spaces, bicycle parking for about 100 bicycles and EV charging, to serve a new swimming pool, nearby homes and planned towers because parking there is insufficient, with use from 1 September 2027 as a target; award and construction were not confirmed [13]. The budget says a deficit of 357,000 euros in 2027, 804,000 in 2028 and 758,000 in 2029 still had to be added for operating it [14]. The council adopted the amended zoning plan for the Oranjerie in July 2024, allowing up to 450 homes and up to 16,000 square metres of centre functions, relying on the existing 517-space garage; its own count is 258 spaces in use plus at most 211 more, 469 in all [12]. The budget also lists real-time parking data, a scan car for enforcement and a study of moving inner-city street parking into garages [15]. Traffic decisions of March and May 2026 reserve spaces for EV charging, naming twelve proactive locations for 2026 [17].

sections.title: Operators, positioning and utilisation
sections.text:
The municipality manages and operates five garages, Marktplein, Haven Centrum, Brinkpark, Anklaar and Orpheus, and six bicycle stores [10]. In 2026 the Marktplein garage costs 2.77 euros an hour by day with a daily maximum of 13.85 euros, Haven Centrum and Brinklaan 1.13 euros an hour with 8.82 euros per 24 hours, and Anklaar is free for 120 minutes [2]. Q-Park lists four sites: Beekstraat with 105 spaces, Museum Centrum with 636, Oranjerie with 519 and the P+R Laan van de Mensenrechten with 188, advertising day rates of 13 and 16.50 euros [8][9]. The 2021 mobility vision counts 5,367 parking spaces in the centre, 3,102 in garages and 2,265 on the street, with pressure at most 50 percent overall but locally above 100 percent [7]. Counts of 2022 around the Oranjerie found the Q-Park garage at 21 percent on a weekday evening and 44 percent on a Saturday afternoon [11].

Our data cover two car parks for about 61 days, from different feeds. The Q-Park Beekstraat garage, with 105 spaces, averaged 71% on weekdays and 76% at weekends and reached full in single readings around midday on Saturdays, so it is the busy one. The P+R Laan van de Mensenrechten (188 spaces), measured for only 18 days, averaged 24% on weekdays and 2% at weekends, a commuter pattern.
